title: Rate Limiting Explained
intro: One buggy client or attacker can flood your API. Rate limiting caps how many requests each client can make.

slides.heading: Why limit?
slides.subtitle: Protect the system for everyone.
slides.explain: Without limits, one script can overload your servers, run up your costs or brute-force passwords. Limits keep the service fair and stable.

slides.heading: Fixed window
slides.subtitle: Count requests per time window.
slides.explain: Allow N requests per minute and reset the count each minute. It's simple, but a burst at the end of one window plus the start of the next can allow double the limit.

slides.heading: Sliding window
slides.subtitle: A smoother count.
slides.explain: Instead of resetting at fixed times, it counts requests over the last rolling minute. This removes the edge-burst problem at the cost of a bit more memory.

slides.heading: Token bucket
slides.subtitle: Allows controlled bursts.
slides.explain: Each client has a bucket that refills with tokens at a steady rate. Every request spends a token; when the bucket is empty, requests are rejected until it refills.

slides.heading: In practice
slides.subtitle: Where it lives and what it returns.
slides.explain: Rate limiting usually sits at the API gateway or load balancer, with counters in a fast shared store like Redis so every server sees the same count.
points: Limit per user, API key or IP

scenario.situation: A login endpoint has no limit on attempts.
scenario.problem: An attacker's script tries thousands of passwords per minute against user accounts.
scenario.fix: Limit each IP and account to 5 attempts per minute with a token bucket in Redis, returning 429 when exceeded. Brute force becomes impractical.
scenario.takeaway: Rate limit every public endpoint, especially login.
